en: The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Youth Śreṇika, translated by the Western Jin śramaṇa Zhi Fadu.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha. It was at dawn.
Accompanied by the bhikṣus, he donned his kāṣāya robe and took up his alms-bowl to enter the city for alms.

As the Buddha approached the gate of Puṣkarasārin, Puṣkarasārin had a son sixteen years of age named Śreṇika. At that time, standing within the third gate, he saw from afar the Buddha approaching; his body possessed extraordinary marks and his countenance was upright and handsome. His mind was serene and his faculties were tranquil. A light radiated from the back of his neck, its brilliance peerless and its radiant glow intensely blazing, like the purity of the sun or the fullness of the moon, illuminating the entire interior of the gate.
Having seen the Buddha in this manner, his heart was filled with joy and he paid him reverent homage. He then hurried up to the hall and spoke a verse for his mother, saying:
“The golden light is a hundredfold; Rare indeed is what I have seen and heard.
Now that I have come to stay outside, I shall provide whatever you require.”
“His majestic deportment surpasses that of Brahmā, and his radiant countenance excels that of all the devas.
He has come here solely out of compassion for me; I pray that you will grant him [this gift].
Hearing Śreṇika’s words, her mother immediately said:
"As you have described him, could such a person truly be poor?
Why would he be a beggar?
How deluded you are!"
"What you have just said is entirely inconsistent with the truth.

At that moment, the Buddha, by means of his supernormal powers, manifested a transformation, emitting a bodily radiance that shone through the seven layers of gates, filling them all with great brilliance.
Moved by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, he again spoke a verse for his mother:
"Just as a person who sees fire Deliberately throws himself into it,
So too is one who acts unwholesomely toward the Buddha A thief unto himself."
Most honored among gods and humans, the Supreme Sage beyond whom there is none;
he is the one most worthy of offerings, and giving to him will surely bring great benefit.
Of the portion of food I now possess, I pray that you take some for yourself and give it to me.
"I wish to offer this to the Honored One; such joy is difficult to encounter again.

His mother then gave him all her fine garments and food provisions. Śreṇika took them and went to where the Buddha was. He prostrated himself with his head to the ground to pay homage to the Buddha, then withdrew to stand to one side. With palms joined, he addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Now that I have seen the Tathāgata, my heart is filled with devotion and reverence as I focus my attention upon the Buddha. I pray only that you will look upon me with compassion and accept what I offer."
The Buddha accepted it at that time and spoke a verse for Śreṣṭha, saying:

"Because you have subdued the mind of stinginess And are able to skillfully cultivate the practice of giving, Today you make offerings to the Buddha; Whatever you intend shall not fail to be auspicious."
Having heard what the Buddha said, Śreṇika immediately spoke this verse himself:
"I do not wish for wealth or nobility, nor do I hope for the status of Śakra or Brahmā;
I only wish for supreme wisdom, like that of the Buddha, unsurpassed."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, descended and stood before Śreṇika, speaking in verse:
"To seek Buddhahood by means of a single act of giving is difficult;
One must practice giving constantly, life after life, Accumulating merit like the jewels of Mount Sumeru."
"Having passed through ten billion kalpas, constantly practicing loving-kindness and compassion,
one cannot attain awakening to the unsurpassed path through a single act of giving alone.
Śāriputra then replied to Śakra, Lord of the Devas, speaking in verse:
"Just as a master craftsman who wishes to fell a giant tree does not cut it down with a single stroke of the axe, but rather fells the great tree by striking gradually;
so too, by chopping little by little, one may exhaust even the timber of Mount Tai."
The karma of peeling away [defilements] is attained from the minute; seeking the Way is likewise so.
It is not by a single act of giving that one attains the Great Way;
yet, possessing faith and diligence, I shall surely become a leader of the world.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, further spoke a verse for Śreṇika:
"It is better to seek the Honored One among the gods;
Indra and Brahmā are easy to attain, but few can respond to the Buddha-dharma, for the path of the Buddha is exceedingly difficult to find."
Gati replied to Śakra, Lord of the Devas, speaking in verse:
"Even if the entire world were filled with blazing fire, I would cast my body into it completely;
I shall never abandon the intent of the Buddha."
Even if all people were to join together to harm me as thieves, may I always maintain a heart of loving-kindness toward them and never abandon the Great Way.
Fragile indeed are the realms of Śakra and Brahmā; they too are subject to the law of death.
"I vow to take refuge in the All-Knowing One, courageous as a lion-like hero.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, further spoke a verse to the *śramaṇa*:
"How wonderful! You have attained a sublime benefit!"
"He possesses reverence for the Buddha and is single-mindedly intent upon the Great Way; I believe you will surely become a Buddha.
Śreṇika replied to Śakra, Lord of the Devas, speaking in verse:
"O Heavenly King, do not harbor doubt regarding this unsurpassed Way."
"With diligence and without indolence, I shall become a Buddha in this world.
Thereupon, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, remained silent.
Then the Buddha spoke these verses for the sake of Gati:
"In past ages, you have reverently served eight thousand Buddhas;
your mind has always aspired to the Great Way, desiring to bring peace to all living beings.
For twelve billion kalpas thereafter, you shall never fall into the evil realms."
But by cultivating many virtues and goodness, you shall always fulfill the noble intention.
You shall become a Cakravartin king ten billion times,
and also serve as a King of the Four Heavenly Kings, each time practicing the True Dharma.
Furthermore, he shall become Śakra, never far from the holy life;
later he will be born in Tuṣita Heaven, and thus his virtue and wisdom will be perfected.
He shall preside over a realm of a thousand lands, and in its center he will attain Buddhahood.
The kalpa was named Sumeru; there was no one who did not serve him.
Each of the thousand kingdoms was four hundred and eighty li in width;
the adornments of the palace walls were all made of precious jewels.
When he first preached the Dharma, sixty thousand koṭis of people were received as disciples and attained liberation; all of them became arhats.
When he preached the sūtra on the second assembly, forty thousand koṭis of people [attained the same].
All have entered the wisdom of Arhats; those delivered by them are exceedingly numerous.
When preaching the sutras during the three assemblies, those delivered are likewise very many;
free from defilement, they enter pure wisdom and all attain non-attachment.
At that time, within the Buddha-field, there were no chaotic or evil beings;
all turned toward the Way and the Dharma, and everyone practiced loyalty and integrity.
Regarding the anxieties and sufferings of illness, such demons were entirely absent.
The people of that time were all harmonious and friendly, looking after one another’s well-being;
the heavens sent rain three times each day, just enough to settle the dust;
cold and heat were always temperate and appropriate, as they delivered countless kinds of beings.
If men and women of noble lineage wish to give rise to wholesome thoughts and cultivate reverence and love for the Buddha, they should make offerings in this manner.
I shall now expound upon this, which is what a bodhisattva ought to practice.
Facing before the Perfectly Awakened One, one immediately attains the Buddha’s eye of wisdom.
The Buddhas are beyond numbering, and the teachings of the sutras are inexhaustible;
if one pays them honor with what is beyond numbering, the karmic reward shall likewise be immeasurable.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this definitive discourse, the son of the householder Śreṣṭhin departed. Having heard the sutra, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and all the bhikṣus rejoiced; they all came forward to pay homage to the Buddha and then withdrew.
The Scripture on the Departure of the Youthful Prince (Gatimāṇavaka-sūtra)
